source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies
finding: Prompting 10 ChatGPT models to reason by recognition-primed decision making (RPD) beat a default prompt on 45 real triage vignettes. A data-frame prompt did similarly.
numbers: 13,500 assessments (10 models x 45 vignettes x 3 prompts x 10 runs). Accuracy: default 63.3% (CI 61.9-64.7), RPD prompt 67.6% (66.3-69), data-frame 66.7% (65.3-68). Mixed logit OR 2.26 (RPD) and 2.05 (data-frame), both p<.001.
limits: One task, one domain, OpenAI models only. Prompts add output tokens and cost. No human users tested.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM test of RPD as a prompt. The gain is real but about 4 points, so treat RPD as one mode, not a big lever.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) per-model and per-class results
finding: The RPD prompt gain was uneven. It helped the weak self-care class most and helped reasoning models more than non-reasoning ones. The newest models showed no gain.
numbers: Self-care accuracy 13.4% default -> 29.8% RPD, 24.6% data-frame. GPT-4.1 self-care 0% -> 43.8% (RPD). Gain larger for reasoning models (OR 2.15 for RPD). GPT-4.1 mini 49.8% -> 60.7% (RPD), 62.4% (data-frame, +13 pts). GPT-5.2 Instant 57.8% -> 56.4% and GPT-5.2 Thinking 52.0% -> 53.1%: no gain. RPD raised accuracy in 18 of 45 cases (40%) and lowered it in 13 (29%).
limits: Emergency class had only 2 cases (98-100% for all prompts), so no safety claim. 88% of errors were over-triage. Gain may shrink as models improve.
agent_relevance: The mode prompt shifted the model's prior (toward less urgency) rather than adding general reasoning. Test per model and gate on a measured gain.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) robustness checks
finding: The RPD gain held in a binary care-vs-self-care recoding and at low temperature. Output variability was the same across the three prompts.
numbers: Same 13,500 runs. Results 'remained similar' in binary choice (Table S1) and low temperature (Table S2). Nonemergency accuracy flat: 82.5% default, 82.0% RPD, 82.8% data-frame.
limits: Authors list cost, single domain and single vendor as limits. The prompt did not reduce variability.
agent_relevance: A prompt-only mode switch does not cut sampling noise; combine with self-consistency if variance matters.

source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo & Griffiths (2024) Mind your step (by step): chain-of-thought can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse
finding: Forced step-by-step reasoning hurts LLMs on the same task types where verbalising hurts people (implicit statistical learning, face recognition, rules with exceptions). This is a boundary condition for 'always deliberate'.
numbers: Artificial grammar learning: o1-preview 57.7% vs GPT-4o zero-shot 94.0% on a 440-problem subset (-36.3 pts); GPT-4o CoT 64.4% vs 87.5% zero-shot (-23.1). Face recognition: GPT-4o 64.0% -> 51.2%, Claude 3 Opus 44.0% -> 29.6%, all 6 multimodal models dropped. Exceptions task: GPT-4o needed 12.5 rounds with CoT vs 2.9 direct (+331%).
limits: 3 of 6 human-failure archetypes transferred; the other 3 did not. Claude 3.5 Sonnet showed almost no CoT penalty.
agent_relevance: Intuition-first modes are justified when the task is pattern-like and hard to put in words. Add a rule to skip written reasoning on such items.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Mind your step: tasks where CoT did not hurt
finding: Not every human failure of deliberation transfers. For logical-inconsistency tasks, models improved with CoT because they hold priors that people lack. Long context helped CoT in a preference-aggregation task.
numbers: Three archetypes showed no consistent CoT drop. Claude 3.5 Sonnet on the grammar task: CoT 67.7% vs zero-shot 65.9% (-1.8 pt drop, i.e. slight gain), p = 0.969.
limits: Per-task results only; no unified moderator model.
agent_relevance: Mode choice must be made per task type and per model, since moderators differ by model.

source: Bossard et al. (2022) Naturalistic decision-making in sport: how current advances into the recognition-primed decision model offer insights
finding: A review quotes a literature summary: most expert decisions in sport are simple-match intuition, a minority need diagnosis or evaluation. It also notes experts choose their preferred first option most of the time.
numbers: Macquet (2020) as quoted: 60-81% of expert decisions simple match; about 13-28% diagnosis; about 3-24% evaluating a course of action. Experts pick their preferred first option in about 80% of decisions.
limits: Secondary quote of Macquet 2020, not the primary data. Time pressure is the stated cause of the intuition share. Self-report and case-study methods dominate.
agent_relevance: A prior for mode choice: most decisions in familiar territory are match; reserve slow checks for the 20-40% that are atypical.

source: Systematic review: Understanding a player's decision-making process in team sports (2021), RPD studies
finding: Of the team-sport studies reviewed, 4 tested RPD and all fit it. Typical situations get a quick match; atypical ones get diagnosis. Level 3 (mental simulation of several options) was rarely verbalised.
numbers: Nine databases searched; 4 RPD studies. Expert hockey and rugby league players showed pattern recognition and little conscious thought in typical play. Two other studies found pattern-matching ability tracked decision accuracy.
limits: Mostly interview and think-aloud data; 'fit' is a loose test since the model has three levels. The review sets RPD against information-processing and ecological-dynamics accounts with no decisive test.
agent_relevance: RPD levels map to modes: match, diagnose, simulate. The rarity of level 3 suggests simulation is the costly mode to reserve.

source: Systematic review of team-sport decision making (2021), deliberation under pressure
finding: Players who consciously deliberate or reinvest in rules under pressure did worse than those who acted on intuition. If-then rule instruction helped transfer to complex tasks while implicit learning did not.
numbers: Raab and Laborde (as cited): deliberating players less successful than intuitive ones. Raab: if-then rule instruction facilitated transfer to relatively complex tasks.
limits: Cited secondhand from the review; no effect sizes in the review text.
agent_relevance: Rule training and pattern exposure serve different transfer needs. Do not force explicit rule recital under load.

source: Belling, Suss & Ward (2014) Advancing theory and application of cognitive research in sport: representative tasks to explain and predict skilled anticipation, decision-making and option generation
finding: Soccer test of take-the-first (TTF) and RPD against long-term working memory (LTWM). Skilled players generated more task-relevant and fewer irrelevant options, which fits LTWM better than 'few options, first is best'. TTF held only partly under time pressure.
numbers: NCAA Division 1 vs recreational players; 30 video simulations, 6 time-constrained and 6 not per phase. Total option count was not significantly related to decision quality (direction as TTF predicted). Time constraint cut only task-irrelevant options, with no skill by time interaction.
limits: Written responses; moderately skilled subject-matter experts as criterion; soccer only. The authors call support for LTWM 'tentative'.
agent_relevance: Do not equate 'good = few options'. Quality-filtered option generation (relevant options early, junk dropped) beats a flat cap on option count.

source: Johnson & Raab (2003) Take the first: option-generation and resulting choices, as summarised in Belling et al. (2014)
finding: Founding take-the-first study: intermediate handball players generated few options, the first was best on average, and more options meant a worse final choice.
numbers: 85 intermediate handball players, 31 video trials, expert panel rated option quality; 2-3 options generated; first option better than later ones; total options negatively related to final quality. Frozen image shown 45 s in 2003, 6 s in the 2007 follow-up.
limits: Not opened directly; read through a secondary summary. Quality rated by experts; frozen final frame is a weak match to live play.
agent_relevance: Source of the few-options generate-test design. Worth testing in an LLM as an option-order effect.

source: Raab & Johnson (2007) and Laborde & Raab (2013), as summarised in Belling et al. (2014)
finding: Extension across skill: experts picked higher-quality final options than near-experts and non-experts. Laborde & Raab: experts generated fewer options than near-experts but not fewer than non-experts, so option count is a weak expertise marker.
numbers: Raab & Johnson 2007 total n = 69 (expert, near-expert, non-expert handball). Laborde & Raab 2013: experts < near-experts in option count; no difference vs non-experts.
limits: Secondhand summary. The non-monotonic option count is a partial failure of the simple 'experts consider fewer options' story.
agent_relevance: Measure the quality of the first option, not option count, when judging the agent's mode.

source: Klein & Peio (1989) chess option generation, as summarised in Belling et al. (2014)
finding: Skilled chess players generated fewer options than less-skilled players (not significant), listed the opponent's actual next move first more often, and predicted it more accurately.
numbers: Direction only; the option-count gap was 'not at a significant level'.
limits: Secondhand; the source summary gives no N. Count difference not significant.
agent_relevance: Supports first-option quality as the expertise signal, with the same caveat as above.

source: Embodied choice in handball: Elite players invest additional time for making better embodied choices (2022)
finding: Contrary to 'experts are faster', elite handball players made the best tactical choice more often but took longer on it.
numbers: 22 elite and 22 amateur handball players, 32 attack sequences. Best choice: elite 44.7% (72) vs amateur 20.8% (32), chi2(1)=20.4, p<.001, V=.25. For best choices elite RT 1,920 ms vs amateur 1,704 ms. Specific-choice distribution differed, chi2(3)=21.5, V=.26. Confidence equal across groups.
limits: Four-option forced choice, not open option generation. Amateurs were older. Best choice defined by a 3-of-4 expert majority rule (experts agreed on 75% of baseline items).
agent_relevance: Expertise showed up as accuracy at similar confidence, with a shift toward accuracy over speed. Do not use speed as a proxy for expert mode.

source: Soccer referees' yellow card decisions: Faster, more accurate, more confident? (2024)
finding: A direct intuitive-versus-analytic manipulation with experts and novices. Analytic style was slightly more accurate overall, but the gain was for novices. Experts did about equally well either way and were more confident when intuitive.
numbers: 60 male referees (30 expert, 30 novice). Intuitive limited to 1,500 ms, analytic to 4,000 ms. Style effect F(1,58)=5.29, p=.025 (analytic 76.3% vs intuitive 74.7%). Expertise F=326.4 (84.3% vs 66.6%). Style x level F=20.09. Experts analytic 83.5% vs intuitive 85.1% (ns); novices 69.0% vs 64.3%. Expert confidence 8.91 (intuitive) vs 8.34 (analytic).
limits: The time cutoffs defining intuitive and analytic were the authors' own. Some reported eta-squared values look inconsistent. Replays at 2x speed.
agent_relevance: Expertise moderates the value of slow thinking: novices gain, experts do not. Experts show more confidence in fast mode, so add a calibration check there.

source: Unconscious thought effect in medical decision making: a critical review and meta-analysis (2015)
finding: No reliable benefit of distraction ('unconscious thought') over deliberation for clinicians' diagnoses. A rival to the view that non-deliberate processing is best for experts.
numbers: Composite-effect meta-analysis d = 0.14, 95% CI [-0.16, 0.43], z = 0.92, p = .36. Expertise moderator Q(1)=5.71, p=.017 but opposite to theory: unconscious thought hurt experts d = -0.14 [-0.32, 0.04] and helped novices d = 0.24 [-0.02, 0.51]. Bayes factors mostly favoured the null; only 3 conditions supported the effect.
limits: Few studies (de Vries 2010; Mamede 2010; Bonke 2014; Woolley 2015). The positive de Vries result did not replicate in Woolley with family physicians. This is not an RPD test, but it tests 'intuition beats deliberation'.
agent_relevance: Do not claim that a pause or incubation step improves expert answers on its own. Treat 'sleep on it' prompts as unproven.

source: Video-based decision-making training for football referees: systematic review and meta-analysis (2025)
finding: Video-scenario training (the same idea as ShadowBox and feedback on realistic cases) improved referees' decision accuracy in randomised trials, with a large but heterogeneous effect.
numbers: 6 RCTs (5 articles), N=163 referees, 1 to 4 weeks, 1-3 sessions per week. Hedges g = 1.718, 95% CI [1.058, 2.377], p<.001, tau2 = 0.464, I2 = 69.6%. No single study changed the result in leave-one-out analysis.
limits: Tiny trials from a few groups, no active control, outcome is accuracy on clips like the training clips. Likely inflated.
agent_relevance: Practice on cases with feedback changes skill. For the agent this argues for case libraries with feedback, not abstract rules.

source: Shadowbox simulation: the rise of shadowbox simulation to illuminate decision-making (2026)
finding: ShadowBox (NDM-based training where learners compare their choices to experts') was adapted to hospital medicine. Evidence is descriptive, with no effect sizes.
numbers: More than 40 sessions in Scotland's internal medicine training. Outcomes are learner satisfaction and perceived retention; no controlled comparison.
limits: Only the abstract and opening sections were read closely. Claims of lower resource use are given without numbers.
agent_relevance: NDM-derived training has little controlled evidence in medicine. Do not cite it as proven for scaffolds.

source: Endorsement of Klein's decision-making assumptions among Norwegian military professionals (2026)
finding: Practitioners mostly hold analytic beliefs that NDM challenges. They endorse generating and comparing options and gathering more information, and are split on intuition and early conclusions.
numbers: N = 225 Norwegian military students; 11 Likert items (1 = strongly agree). Q4 'generate several options and compare' M=1.88; Q5 'collect more information reduces uncertainty' M=1.83; Q3 'rely on logic not intuition' M=3.00; Q6 'bad to draw early conclusions' M=3.04. EFA: two factors (planning/structure, analytic/evidence), 29.24% variance, alpha .65 and .71; 3 items dropped; KMO .741.
limits: Attitude survey, not behaviour. Items were never built as a scale. One country, one school.
agent_relevance: Even trained operators prefer the analytic recipe. An LLM trained on their writing may default to compare-options even where NDM says not to.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: Joint paper by the heuristics-and-biases camp and the NDM camp. Intuition can be trusted only if the environment is regular enough to be predictable and the person had enough practice with feedback to learn it.
numbers: No numbers. Two conditions: valid environmental cues, and an opportunity to learn them.
limits: Full text not opened (publisher and mirror pages were blocked or needed login); abstract summary seen only via search. Klein later said they disagreed a lot.
agent_relevance: Core boundary rule for mode choice: trust fast recognition only where cues are valid and the model has had feedback; otherwise force checking.

source: Klein, Calderwood & Clinton-Cirocco (1986) Rapid decision making on the fire ground, as described in a 2016 Frontiers perspective
finding: Original RPD fireground finding. The perspective says RPD accounted for 80-90% of firefighters' decisions and needed 10-20 years of experience to develop; it cites follow-ups in military leaders, offshore oil managers and VR firefighting.
numbers: '80-90% of the decisions firefighters made' (no citation on the sentence, no N). Follow-ups listed: Schmitt & Klein 1999, Skriver 1998 (thesis), Keren et al. 2013 (VR). 1986 paper: Human Factors Society proceedings 30(6): 576-580.
limits: Original not opened. Perspective is coauthored by Klein and presents no new data. A figure of 156 decisions and 80% could not be verified. The share comes from coding interview recall.
agent_relevance: The founding number rests on retrospective interviews coded by the model's authors; treat as a prior, not an effect size.

source: Lipshitz, Klein, Orasanu & Salas (2001) Taking stock of naturalistic decision making, as described in the 2016 Frontiers perspective
finding: The main critique: NDM's field methods lack control. The lead article drew 16 commentaries; the NDM community argued controlled lab conditions would remove the object of study.
numbers: 16 commentaries in Journal of Behavioral Decision Making. No effect sizes.
limits: Original not opened; described secondhand. The dispute between rigour and realism was not settled by a decisive test.
agent_relevance: The lack of controlled tests is why LLM experiments like Kopka & Feufel are among the few clean comparisons.

source: Wikipedia: Naturalistic decision-making
finding: NDM aims at limited time, uncertainty, high stakes, unstable conditions and varying experience. Lab replication of high stakes and extreme expertise is hard, so field methods are used.
numbers: No empirical numbers. First conference 1989 in Dayton, Ohio; book Klein, Orasanu, Calderwood, Zsambok 1993.
limits: Encyclopedia text, not a study.
agent_relevance: Used only for scope.

source: Wikipedia: Recognition-primed decision
finding: States RPD needs extensive experience and fails in unusual or misidentified circumstances; novices cycle through possibilities and use the first workable action.
numbers: None. Sourced only to Klein, Sources of Power (1998).
limits: No replication evidence on the page; carries a 'needs citations' banner.
agent_relevance: The key failure is a wrong match giving a confident wrong action. Needs a mismatch check.

source: Evaluating the o1 reasoning large language model for cognitive bias: a vignette study (2025)
finding: o1 showed fewer human-like biases than GPT-4 and clinicians in 10 clinical vignettes, but failed badly on a few. Deliberative reasoning cuts many biases in an LLM and still fails on specific ones.
numbers: 1,800 responses (90 per vignette version x 10 biases). No significant bias in 7 of 10. Hindsight bias difference 52.2 pts (GPT-4 85, clinicians 56); post hoc fallacy 17.8 (GPT-4 56, clinicians 47); Occam's razor 100 pts (full reversal), larger than both. Within-version agreement above 94% in 8 of 10 scenarios.
limits: Vignette pairs come from earlier studies; the comparison numbers are from prior papers. Possible training-data contamination.
agent_relevance: Keep targeted checks for biases that reasoning does not fix.

source: Exposing the fragility of LLM reasoning through bias-inducing prompts: BiasMedQA (2026)
finding: Reasoning variants were more accurate but not consistently less biased. A debiasing instruction and few-shot examples reduced biased answers in all three models.
numbers: 1,273 vignettes, 7 biases. Llama-3.3-70B 72.5-82.1% reasoning vs 61.0-73.4%; Qwen3-32B 71.7-78.7% vs 55.5-64.1%; Gemini-2.5-Flash 81.8-88.6% vs 80.0-83.7%. Reasoning OR for correct: 4.0, 3.6, 3.2. On 4 unpublished bias prompts Gemini fell to 47.4-86.1%; biased share 49.9% (reasoning) vs 16.7% (not); debiasing prompt cut this to 18.5%; few-shot to about 5%.
limits: Possible contamination of the public set. Few-shot prompts show the bias pattern itself.
agent_relevance: Slow mode alone is not safe. Few-shot examples of the failure beat a generic 'be careful' line; this is the same idea as learning from cases.

source: Detecting expertise in decision making under pressure: VR-DMX virtual reality assessment (2026)
finding: A new test of decision quality under time limits separates individuals and is distinct from general ability, but it is not yet tied to real experts.
numbers: Two validation studies, N=60 and N=76. Coefficients of variation 32.4-37.4% (Total Tickets) and 20.8-27.6% (DMX score). Meta-analytic correlation of the two metrics r = 0.771 (95% CI 0.599-0.943). Study 1 tickets M=1509, SD=489.
limits: Not yet compared with professionals. Arcade task, not a field task. Validity vs real expertise unproven.
agent_relevance: Shows time-pressure allocation skill can be measured; a possible template for scoring an agent's mode switching.

source: Old wine in a new bottle: are different terminologies on dual processing conceptually the same? (2026)
finding: Terms like intuition vs analysis, System 1 vs 2 and RPD vs analytic are lexically different but conceptually close (the jangle fallacy).
numbers: BERT-based similarity analysis plus a thought experiment; no human sample in the abstract.
limits: Read the abstract and introduction only. Overlapping labels do not prove the same mechanism.
agent_relevance: Use one shared mode vocabulary in the scaffold; do not stack 'intuitive', 'recognitional' and 'System 1' as separate switches.

source: Long-term working memory (Ericsson & Kintsch 1995) as a rival to RPD, tested in Belling et al. (2014)
finding: Rival theory to RPD: experts build a situation model that indexes many relevant options, so they do not hold fewer options, they hold better-organised ones. Discriminating prediction: more task-relevant options help, irrelevant options hurt.
numbers: Skilled players generated more task-relevant and fewer task-irrelevant options (factorial ANOVA), and both counts predicted anticipation and decision quality in regression.
limits: One study, one sport; the authors still say take-the-first holds in the intervention phase under time pressure.
agent_relevance: A discriminating test the agent could run: count relevant versus irrelevant candidate actions in traces, not total candidates.
